subtopic_detail: First line therapy for primary monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis after conservative measures
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 7 year old boy brought in by his mother for ongoing bedwetting. He has never been reliably dry at night. Days are dry. There is no daytime urgency, dysuria or straining. He empties his bladder before bed. Fluid intake is limited after 5 pm and caffeine free. He has no constipation, no snoring or sleep disordered breathing, no polydipsia by day and no history suggestive of urinary tract infection. Development is normal, school performance is normal and there is no psychosocial red flag. He is otherwise well.

He has already tried a star chart with reward for dry mornings for 3 months without improvement. His mother is asking about further options because he wants to attend his first school camp in 6 weeks. There is a family history of paternal childhood bedwetting until age 10 years.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88 /min, blood pressure 98/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Examination: Growth on 50th centile height and weight, abdomen soft with no palpable bladder or faecal mass, lumbosacral spine unremarkable, lower limb neurology intact
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick negative, morning first pass urine osmolality 720 mOsm/kg (>800 suggests normal concentrating ability), no other investigations indicated

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first line treatment strategy now given his upcoming school camp?

options.text: Continue reward chart with delayed fluid restriction pushed to 6 pm and review outcomes in 3 months at general practice
options.rationale: Reward charts alone have already failed after a 3 month trial; escalation to an active therapy is indicated with a defined event in 6 weeks. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline on Enuresis)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline on Enuresis

options.text: Bedwetting enuresis alarm nightly for at least 8 weeks as the durable first line therapy, teach parents the wake protocol
options.rationale: Enuresis alarms are the most effective first line therapy for durable cure (evidence based number needed to treat around 2) but need at least 8 weeks and are not suited to a 6 week camp deadline. Explain benefits and offer as durable therapy after the camp. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline on Enuresis)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline on Enuresis

options.text: Oral oxybutynin 5 mg at bedtime as a first line therapy for primary monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis at this age
options.rationale: Anticholinergics are used in enuresis with detrusor overactivity or when desmopressin plus alarm have failed; they are not first line for primary monosymptomatic enuresis. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline on Enuresis)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline on Enuresis

options.text: Oral desmopressin 120 microg sublingual wafer at bedtime as short term cover only for the camp, plan an alarm afterwards
options.rationale: In primary monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis at age 7 with a specific short term social need (camp in 6 weeks), desmopressin sublingual wafer 120 microg (or 200 microg tablet) at bedtime with strict evening fluid restriction is the recommended short term option; the durable therapy is an enuresis alarm and should be planned once the deadline passes. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline on Enuresis)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline on Enuresis

options.text: Refer to paediatric urology for cystometry to exclude posterior urethral valves and detrusor overactivity before any treatment
options.rationale: Urodynamics is not indicated in primary monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis with a normal examination and negative urinalysis; workup can be entirely non invasive. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline on Enuresis)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline on Enuresis

explanation.summary: Primary monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis in a school aged child is treated after conservative measures (reward chart, fluid timing, constipation exclusion, sleep disordered breathing exclusion) fail. Two first line active therapies are enuresis alarm (highest sustained cure rate but 8 to 12 weeks to work) and desmopressin (rapid response, useful for camps or sleepovers, but relapse on cessation is common). A specific short deadline favours desmopressin cover with a plan for the alarm afterwards. Anticholinergics are reserved for detrusor overactivity or combined therapy after first line failure.
key_points: Enuresis alarm is the highest sustained cure rate therapy but needs 8 to 12 weeks to work.
Desmopressin 120 microg sublingual wafer (or 200 microg tablet) at bedtime is preferred for short term cover such as camps.
Anticholinergics are reserved for detrusor overactivity or combination therapy after first line failure.
explanation.pearls: For a 6 week camp deadline: desmopressin 120 microg sublingual wafer at bedtime with strict evening fluid restriction; plan an enuresis alarm as durable therapy after the camp.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline on Enuresis
International Children's Continence Society standardisation on monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis

subtopic_detail: Neonatal testicular torsion presenting on day 2 of life with a firm hemiscrotal mass
stem:
You are the paediatric surgery registrar reviewing a term male neonate on day 2 of life at his post natal check. The midwife has noted a firm, non tender, discoloured left hemiscrotum since birth. He was born by uncomplicated vaginal birth at 39 weeks, birthweight 3.4 kg, Apgar scores 9 and 9. He is feeding well and voiding urine normally. He has passed meconium. The right testis and cord are palpable and normal. The left hemiscrotum is bluish, swollen and firm; the underlying testis cannot be distinguished from surrounding oedema. There is no scrotal skin loss.

Scrotal ultrasound with colour Doppler shows an enlarged, heterogeneous left testis with absent intratesticular blood flow and an intact right testis with normal Doppler. He has not been fed for 2 hours and is otherwise well. Parents have been counselled about torsion. Anaesthetics have been notified.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148 /min, blood pressure 62/38 mmHg, respiratory rate 42 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 degC
data_table.Examination: Bluish oedematous firm non tender left hemiscrotum from birth, right testis palpable and normal, cremasteric reflex not reliably assessable at this age
data_table.Investigations: Scrotal ultrasound left testis enlarged heterogeneous with absent intratesticular Doppler flow, right testis normal Doppler; urinalysis clean; full blood count and C reactive protein within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate operative plan?

options.text: Manual detorsion at the cotside now under nitrous oxide gas analgesia by the paediatric surgery registrar attending
options.rationale: Manual detorsion is not appropriate in the neonate; the neonatal scrotum requires operative exploration. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Neonatal Surgical Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Neonatal Surgical Guideline

options.text: Observation with warm compresses and repeat scrotal ultrasound in 24 hours before deciding on any further operative intervention
options.rationale: Observation risks loss of the contralateral testis if bell clapper anatomy is present; contralateral fixation is prioritised. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Neonatal Surgical Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Neonatal Surgical Guideline

options.text: Urgent scrotal exploration with left orchidectomy for a necrotic testis and contralateral orchidopexy of the right testis at the same operation
options.rationale: Neonatal torsion presenting at birth with a firm discoloured testis and absent Doppler flow is almost always non salvageable prenatal or perinatal torsion. Contralateral orchidopexy at the same operation is essential because bell clapper anatomy is often bilateral, risking metachronous torsion of the only remaining testis. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Neonatal Surgical Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Neonatal Surgical Guideline

options.text: Semi urgent scrotal exploration within the next few days for a left orchidectomy alone without contralateral fixation of the right testis
options.rationale: Contralateral orchidopexy is essential because bell clapper anatomy is often bilateral; failing to fix the right testis risks metachronous torsion. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Neonatal Surgical Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Neonatal Surgical Guideline

options.text: Doppler ultrasound repeated at 6 hours and 12 hours as the sole investigation before any decision about operative theatre in this baby
options.rationale: Serial imaging delays care; the plan is defined by the clinical finding of a firm, discoloured neonatal testis and absent Doppler flow. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Neonatal Surgical Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Neonatal Surgical Guideline

explanation.summary: Neonatal testicular torsion often occurs prenatally or perinatally; the testis at birth is typically necrotic and non salvageable. The critical clinical decision is not testicular salvage but protection of the contralateral testis by fixation at the same operation. Bell clapper anatomy predisposes to bilateral torsion and metachronous loss. Ultrasound with Doppler helps confirm loss of flow but does not delay operative planning. Post operatively, parents require counselling about fertility, testosterone monitoring at puberty and consideration of testicular prosthesis at adolescence.
key_points: Neonatal torsion at birth is almost always non salvageable prenatal torsion.
Contralateral orchidopexy at the same operation is the critical intervention because bell clapper anatomy is often bilateral.
Repeat imaging delays care and does not change the plan of urgent exploration and fixation.
explanation.pearls: Neonatal firm blue hemiscrotum with absent Doppler flow: urgent scrotal exploration; left orchidectomy plus right orchidopexy to protect the contralateral testis from metachronous torsion.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Neonatal Surgical Guideline
American Urological Association guideline on testicular torsion in the neonate

subtopic_detail: Uncomplicated acute otitis externa in a swimmer with intact tympanic membrane
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 12 year old competitive swimmer with 4 days of increasing left ear pain and itching. She reports pain worsened by chewing and by pulling on the pinna. There is no fever, no hearing loss beyond mild muffling, no vertigo and no facial weakness. She has no diabetes, no immunosuppression, no history of tympanostomy tubes and no history of tympanic membrane perforation. She has been in the pool 6 days per week for 12 months. She has not used cotton buds in the last month.

Examination shows a swollen erythematous ear canal with cheesy debris. The tympanic membrane is normal after clearing the debris under otoscopy. She is otherwise well. She has no penicillin allergy and no quinolone allergy. Her parents are asking about treatment.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78 /min, blood pressure 108/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 degC
data_table.Examination: Tender tragus and pinna, oedematous erythematous left external auditory canal with cheesy debris, tympanic membrane intact after debris clearance, no post auricular tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Not indicated in uncomplicated otitis externa with intact tympanic membrane; culture reserved for treatment failure or immunocompromise

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first line therapy?

options.text: Oral amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 5 days plus oral paracetamol as required for pain relief at home
options.rationale: Systemic antibiotics are not first line for uncomplicated otitis externa; topical therapy achieves higher local concentrations. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Otitis externa)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Otitis externa

options.text: Aural toilet plus topical ciprofloxacin plus dexamethasone ear drops for 7 days and pool avoidance until symptoms resolve
options.rationale: First line therapy for acute otitis externa with intact tympanic membrane in AU per Therapeutic Guidelines is aural toilet (wick or microsuction) plus topical ciprofloxacin 0.3 percent plus dexamethasone 0.1 percent 5 drops twice daily for 7 days, with pool avoidance until symptoms resolve. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Otitis externa)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Otitis externa

options.text: Aluminium acetate ear drops alone for 5 days and reassess in 2 weeks if there is no meaningful improvement in her ear pain
options.rationale: Aluminium acetate has some effect but topical antimicrobial therapy is more effective; it is not first line monotherapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Otitis externa)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Otitis externa

options.text: Warm saline irrigation with a bulb syringe by the parents at home twice daily for a week and ibuprofen for pain relief only
options.rationale: Irrigation risks worsening the canal maceration; aural toilet by trained personnel plus topical antibiotic is required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Otitis externa)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Otitis externa

options.text: Oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for 7 days plus paracetamol as required and pool avoidance until symptoms fully settle
options.rationale: Oral ciprofloxacin is reserved for otitis externa with cellulitis extending beyond the canal, malignant (necrotising) otitis externa, or refractory disease; it is not first line. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Otitis externa)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Otitis externa

explanation.summary: Acute otitis externa is diagnosed clinically by canal inflammation and tragal or pinna tenderness. First line therapy in AU per Therapeutic Guidelines is aural toilet plus a topical antimicrobial with a corticosteroid such as ciprofloxacin plus dexamethasone ear drops, with pool avoidance until symptoms resolve. Systemic antibiotics are added for cellulitis spread beyond the canal. Necrotising otitis externa is suspected in diabetics or immunocompromised patients with severe pain, granulation tissue at the bony cartilaginous junction, or cranial nerve palsy; it needs urgent ear nose throat specialist review, imaging and intravenous ciprofloxacin. If the tympanic membrane is perforated or grommets are present, an aminoglycoside containing drop is avoided.
key_points: First line: aural toilet plus topical ciprofloxacin plus dexamethasone ear drops for 7 days.
Oral antibiotics only if cellulitis extends beyond the canal or in immunocompromise.
Avoid aminoglycoside drops with perforated tympanic membrane or grommets.
explanation.pearls: Uncomplicated acute otitis externa with intact tympanic membrane: aural toilet plus topical ciprofloxacin plus dexamethasone 5 drops twice daily for 7 days, plus pool avoidance until symptoms resolve.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Otitis externa
American Academy of Otolaryngology Clinical Practice Guideline on Acute Otitis Externa

subtopic_detail: Metformin candidacy in adolescent obesity with impaired glucose regulation
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 14 year old girl with a body mass index of 34 kg/m^2 (>99.5th centile for age). She has completed a 6 month structured lifestyle programme in primary care with a dietitian and exercise physiologist, with a modest weight increase and no meaningful metabolic improvement. She has acanthosis nigricans around the neck, blood pressure 132/82 mmHg (>95th centile). She has no polyuria, no polydipsia, no visual symptoms and no snoring or sleep disordered breathing. Menarche was at age 12 years and cycles are regular. She has no family history of type 2 diabetes.

Recent investigations show fasting glucose 6.2 mmol/L, haemoglobin A1c 6.1 percent, oral glucose tolerance 2 hour glucose 9.4 mmol/L (7.8-11.0 impaired). Fasting lipids demonstrate low high density lipoprotein cholesterol 0.9 mmol/L, triglycerides 1.8 mmol/L. Liver function tests show mild transaminitis. She has been on no medication.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76 /min, blood pressure 132/82 mmHg (>95th centile for age), respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degC
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 34 kg/m^2, acanthosis nigricans neck and axillae, Tanner stage 5, no striae, no hirsutism
data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 6.2 mmol/L, haemoglobin A1c 6.1 percent, oral glucose tolerance 2 hour glucose 9.4 mmol/L (impaired), alanine aminotransferase 62 U/L, total cholesterol 4.9 mmol/L

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy addition to intensified lifestyle interventions?

options.text: Bariatric surgery referral for consideration of sleeve gastrectomy in every adolescent with body mass index above 34 kg/m^2 alone
options.rationale: Bariatric surgery is considered after failure of intensified pharmacological and lifestyle programmes and typically at body mass index >=40 or >=35 with severe comorbidity; not first line here. (Source: Endocrine Society Paediatric Obesity Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Paediatric Obesity Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Orlistat 120 mg with meals as first line pharmacotherapy in every adolescent with obesity above the 99th body mass index centile
options.rationale: Orlistat is not first line pharmacotherapy for adolescent obesity with impaired glucose regulation; metformin is preferred when dysglycaemia is present. (Source: Endocrine Society Paediatric Obesity Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Paediatric Obesity Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Liraglutide 3 mg subcutaneously daily as first line pharmacotherapy in every adolescent with a body mass index above 30 kg/m^2
options.rationale: Liraglutide 3 mg is TGA registered for adolescent obesity from age 12 but is not first line for impaired glucose regulation and access via the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme is limited. (Source: Endocrine Society Paediatric Obesity Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Paediatric Obesity Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Insulin glargine subcutaneously at bedtime 10 units nocte with continued lifestyle intervention and outpatient endocrinology review
options.rationale: Insulin is inappropriate for impaired glucose regulation without established diabetes; metformin is the recommended first line pharmacotherapy. (Source: Endocrine Society Paediatric Obesity Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Paediatric Obesity Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Metformin extended release 500 mg daily titrated to 2 g daily by 4 weeks, with continued intensified lifestyle intervention
options.rationale: Metformin is a recommended adjunct to lifestyle intervention in adolescents 10 years and older with obesity and impaired glucose regulation (impaired fasting glucose or impaired glucose tolerance, or haemoglobin A1c 5.7 to 6.4 percent) when lifestyle alone is inadequate. Titration from 500 mg daily to 2 g daily over 4 weeks is standard. (Source: Endocrine Society Paediatric Obesity Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Paediatric Obesity Clinical Practice Guideline

explanation.summary: Metformin is a recommended adjunct to intensified lifestyle intervention in adolescents (10 years or older) with obesity and impaired glucose regulation, defined as impaired fasting glucose 6.1 to 6.9 mmol/L, impaired glucose tolerance (2 hour 7.8 to 11.0 mmol/L), or haemoglobin A1c 5.7 to 6.4 percent, when lifestyle alone is inadequate. Standard titration is extended release 500 mg daily up to 2 g daily over 4 weeks. Liraglutide 3 mg is TGA registered from age 12 for adolescent obesity but is not first line for dysglycaemia. Bariatric surgery is reserved for body mass index over 40 or over 35 with severe comorbidity after failed intensive therapy. Screen for polycystic ovary syndrome, non alcoholic fatty liver disease and obstructive sleep apnoea.
key_points: Metformin is first line pharmacotherapy in adolescent obesity with impaired glucose regulation after failed lifestyle intervention.
Titrate extended release 500 mg daily up to 2 g daily over 4 weeks.
Bariatric surgery: body mass index >=40 or >=35 with severe comorbidity after failed intensive medical therapy.
explanation.pearls: Adolescent obesity with impaired glucose tolerance after failed 6 month lifestyle programme: add metformin extended release 500 mg daily titrated to 2 g daily over 4 weeks alongside continued lifestyle intervention.

sources.label: Endocrine Society Paediatric Obesity Clinical Practice Guideline
Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Obesity in Children Clinical Practice Guideline

subtopic_detail: Steroid sensitive nephrotic syndrome first relapse definition and next line therapy after multiple relapses
stem:
You are the paediatric nephrology registrar reviewing a 5 year old boy previously diagnosed with steroid sensitive minimal change nephrotic syndrome 8 months ago. He responded to prednisolone 60 mg/m^2/day and was weaned over 12 weeks. He is now presenting with his fourth relapse, characterised by urine protein creatinine ratio 620 mg/mmol, serum albumin 22 g/L, mild periorbital oedema, no macroscopic haematuria, no hypertension and no renal impairment. Previous three relapses each responded to prednisolone within 10 days. He has now developed steroid toxicity: weight z score up 3 SD from baseline, striae, cushingoid facies, and cataract review pending.

He is otherwise well. He is up to date with immunisations and had varicella infection as a toddler. He is on no other medication. His parents are keen to reduce steroid exposure.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96 /min, blood pressure 108/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.9 degC
data_table.Examination: Periorbital oedema, cushingoid facies, striae over abdomen, tanner stage 1, blood pressure at 75th centile
data_table.Investigations: Urine protein creatinine ratio 620 mg/mmol, serum albumin 22 g/L, creatinine 32 micromol/L, complement C3 and C4 normal, antinuclear antibody negative, hepatitis B and C negative, HIV negative

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate steroid sparing agent to add now given his frequent relapsing and steroid toxic pattern?

options.text: Rituximab 375 mg/m^2 intravenously as a single dose escalation strategy before oral steroid sparing agent trial is initiated
options.rationale: Rituximab is reserved for complicated frequently relapsing or steroid dependent nephrotic syndrome that has failed a conventional steroid sparing oral agent; it is not first line here. (Source: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline on Glomerular Diseases)
source_refs: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline on Glomerular Diseases

options.text: Increase prednisolone to 60 mg/m^2/day induction and prolonged 12 week wean without additional steroid sparing agent added
options.rationale: Continued repeated steroid courses without a sparing agent worsen the established steroid toxicity; a steroid sparing agent is indicated. (Source: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline on Glomerular Diseases)
source_refs: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline on Glomerular Diseases

options.text: Percutaneous renal biopsy urgently to exclude focal segmental glomerulosclerosis before a steroid sparing agent is trialled
options.rationale: Steroid sensitive nephrotic syndrome with prompt response does not require biopsy before a steroid sparing trial; biopsy is considered if steroid resistant or atypical features are present. (Source: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline on Glomerular Diseases)
source_refs: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline on Glomerular Diseases

options.text: Cyclophosphamide 2 mg/kg/day oral for 12 weeks alongside a prednisolone induction and taper for the current fourth relapse
options.rationale: Frequently relapsing (>=2 relapses in 6 months or >=4 in 12 months) or steroid dependent nephrotic syndrome with steroid toxicity is an indication for a steroid sparing agent alongside a fresh steroid induction. Oral cyclophosphamide 2 mg/kg/day for 8 to 12 weeks (cumulative dose limit 168 mg/kg) is a standard KDIGO first line steroid sparing option; levamisole (where available), calcineurin inhibitors and mycophenolate mofetil are alternatives. (Source: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline on Glomerular Diseases)
source_refs: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline on Glomerular Diseases

options.text: Chronic angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor with lisinopril 5 mg daily as monotherapy in place of steroid based induction
options.rationale: Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors are antiproteinuric adjuncts, not induction therapy for active nephrotic relapse; induction plus steroid sparing is required. (Source: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline on Glomerular Diseases)
source_refs: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline on Glomerular Diseases

explanation.summary: Frequently relapsing steroid sensitive nephrotic syndrome is defined as at least 2 relapses in 6 months or at least 4 in 12 months, and steroid dependent as relapse during steroid taper or within 2 weeks of stopping. Both are indications for a steroid sparing agent alongside a fresh steroid induction, particularly if steroid toxicity is established. First line steroid sparing options in KDIGO are oral cyclophosphamide 2 mg/kg/day for 8 to 12 weeks (cumulative dose limit 168 mg/kg), levamisole where available, calcineurin inhibitors and mycophenolate mofetil. Rituximab is reserved for complicated cases after failure of a conventional steroid sparing agent. Renal biopsy is not required before a steroid sparing trial in typical steroid sensitive disease.
key_points: Frequently relapsing nephrotic syndrome: >=2 relapses in 6 months or >=4 in 12 months.
Steroid sparing options include cyclophosphamide, levamisole, calcineurin inhibitors and mycophenolate mofetil.
Rituximab reserved for complicated disease after conventional agents fail.
explanation.pearls: Fourth relapse with steroid toxicity: prednisolone induction and taper alongside cyclophosphamide 2 mg/kg/day for 8 to 12 weeks (cumulative dose limit 168 mg/kg) as the steroid sparing agent.

sources.label: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline on Glomerular Diseases
Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Nephrotic Syndrome Clinical Practice Guideline

subtopic_detail: Differentiating multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children from Kawasaki disease at initial workup
stem:
You are the paediatric inpatient registrar admitting an 8 year old girl with 5 days of fever, non purulent bilateral conjunctivitis, cracked lips, a diffuse maculopapular rash, extremity oedema and cervical lymphadenopathy. She is haemodynamically stable but tachycardic. She had SARS-CoV-2 infection 5 weeks ago (confirmed by household polymerase chain reaction). She has abdominal pain and diarrhoea. Cardiac auscultation is normal. There is no history of allergic contact and no drug exposure.

Investigations show C reactive protein 210 mg/L, ferritin 850 microg/L, N terminal pro brain natriuretic peptide 3200 ng/L, troponin I 45 ng/L (normal <15), lymphocyte count 0.7 x10^9/L, platelets 128 x10^9/L, SARS-CoV-2 IgG positive, polymerase chain reaction negative. Echocardiogram shows mild left ventricular systolic dysfunction (ejection fraction 48 percent) without coronary artery aneurysm. Blood cultures pending.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128 /min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 /min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 39.2 degC
data_table.Examination: Non purulent bilateral conjunctivitis, cracked lips, diffuse maculopapular rash, extremity oedema, unilateral cervical lymphadenopathy 2 cm, abdomen soft with generalised tenderness
data_table.Investigations: C reactive protein 210 mg/L, ferritin 850 microg/L, troponin I 45 ng/L, N terminal pro brain natriuretic peptide 3200 ng/L, lymphocytes 0.7 x10^9/L, platelets 128 x10^9/L, SARS-CoV-2 IgG positive, echocardiogram ejection fraction 48%

lead_in: Which feature most strongly favours multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children over classic Kawasaki disease?

options.text: The presence of bilateral non purulent conjunctivitis is a feature that alone favours multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children over Kawasaki disease
options.rationale: Bilateral non purulent conjunctivitis is a classic feature of both conditions and does not discriminate. (Source: CDC Case Definition for Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children)
source_refs: CDC Case Definition for Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children

options.text: Older age at presentation, prominent abdominal features, lymphopenia and cardiac dysfunction with elevated troponin favour multisystem inflammatory syndrome
options.rationale: Multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children typically presents in older children (median 8 to 10 years), with prominent gastrointestinal features, lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia early, myocardial dysfunction with elevated troponin, and a recent SARS-CoV-2 exposure or seropositivity. Classic Kawasaki disease is a disease of children under 5 with a normal or elevated platelet count and coronary artery aneurysm rather than global left ventricular dysfunction as the cardiac lesion. (Source: CDC Case Definition for Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children)
source_refs: CDC Case Definition for Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children

options.text: Fever for 5 days and a rash on the trunk are features that alone favour multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children over Kawasaki disease
options.rationale: Fever and rash are shared features; they do not discriminate. (Source: CDC Case Definition for Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children)
source_refs: CDC Case Definition for Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children

options.text: Cervical lymphadenopathy above 1.5 cm and cracked lips are features that alone favour multisystem inflammatory syndrome over Kawasaki disease
options.rationale: Cervical lymphadenopathy above 1.5 cm and mucous membrane changes are shared features of both conditions; not discriminatory. (Source: CDC Case Definition for Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children)
source_refs: CDC Case Definition for Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children

options.text: The presence of extremity oedema and rash are features that alone favour multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children over Kawasaki disease
options.rationale: Extremity oedema and rash are classic Kawasaki disease features and do not discriminate multisystem inflammatory syndrome. (Source: CDC Case Definition for Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children)
source_refs: CDC Case Definition for Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children

explanation.summary: Multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children is defined by fever, laboratory evidence of inflammation, evidence of multiorgan involvement (cardiac, renal, respiratory, haematological, gastrointestinal, dermatological or neurological), recent SARS-CoV-2 exposure or seropositivity, and exclusion of alternative diagnoses. It typically presents in older children (median 8 to 10 years) with prominent gastrointestinal symptoms, lymphopenia, elevated ferritin and troponin, and myocardial dysfunction. Kawasaki disease occurs mainly in children under 5, with normal or elevated platelet count and coronary artery aneurysm as the classic cardiac lesion. Initial management shares intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg but multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children also uses methylprednisolone and consideration of anakinra or infliximab in refractory cases.
key_points: Multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children: older age, prominent gastrointestinal features, lymphopenia, elevated troponin, myocardial dysfunction.
Kawasaki disease: median age under 5, normal or elevated platelets, coronary artery aneurysm on echocardiogram.
Both treated with intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg; multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children adds methylprednisolone.
explanation.pearls: Multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children differentiators: older age (median 8 to 10 years), prominent gastrointestinal features, lymphopenia, elevated troponin, myocardial dysfunction rather than coronary aneurysm, plus recent SARS-CoV-2 exposure or IgG positivity.

sources.label: CDC Case Definition for Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children
American College of Rheumatology Clinical Guidance for Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children

subtopic_detail: Neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia recognition with severe thrombocytopenia at birth
stem:
You are the neonatal registrar reviewing a term male infant delivered by uncomplicated vaginal birth at 39 weeks. Birthweight 3.2 kg. He was noted at 6 hours of age to have widespread petechiae over his trunk and limbs and a small subgaleal haematoma. He has no bleeding from cannula sites. His mother is a first time mother with no history of thrombocytopenia and platelet count 285 x10^9/L at booking. She had no pre-eclampsia, no HELLP syndrome, no infection and has taken no antiplatelet medication. Cord blood group is A positive; maternal group A positive.

Investigations at 8 hours of life show platelet count 15 x10^9/L (150-450), haemoglobin 168 g/L, white cell count 12 x10^9/L, C reactive protein 4 mg/L. Blood film shows normal platelet morphology and no schistocytes. Coagulation profile is within normal limits. Cranial ultrasound has been performed as urgent screening and shows no intraventricular haemorrhage. Human platelet antigen genotyping for the infant and both parents has been sent.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148 /min, blood pressure 68/42 mmHg, respiratory rate 44 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.9 degC
data_table.Examination: Petechiae over trunk and limbs, small subgaleal haematoma, anterior fontanelle soft and flat, no organomegaly, no dysmorphic features
data_table.Investigations: Platelet count 15 x10^9/L, haemoglobin 168 g/L, white cell count 12 x10^9/L, C reactive protein 4 mg/L, coagulation profile within normal limits, cranial ultrasound no intraventricular haemorrhage

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate transfusion strategy?

options.text: Transfuse human platelet antigen matched (HPA-1a negative if unknown) platelets plus intravenous immunoglobulin 1 g/kg immediately
options.rationale: Suspected neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia with severe thrombocytopenia (<30 x10^9/L) is treated with human platelet antigen matched platelet transfusion (HPA-1a negative if the antigen is unknown, since HPA-1a is the most common alloantigen in Caucasian populations), plus intravenous immunoglobulin 1 g/kg to reduce further platelet destruction and prolong response duration. (Source: British Society for Haematology Guideline on Neonatal Alloimmune Thrombocytopenia)
source_refs: British Society for Haematology Guideline on Neonatal Alloimmune Thrombocytopenia

options.text: Transfuse random donor platelets 10 mL/kg immediately as the sole intervention without considering intravenous immunoglobulin
options.rationale: Random donor platelets are consumed by the maternal antibody within hours; the response is transient and poor. Human platelet antigen matched platelets are preferred. (Source: British Society for Haematology Guideline on Neonatal Alloimmune Thrombocytopenia)
source_refs: British Society for Haematology Guideline on Neonatal Alloimmune Thrombocytopenia

options.text: Transfuse maternal washed platelets collected by apheresis today plus corticosteroid (prednisolone 2 mg/kg/day oral) at commencement
options.rationale: Maternal platelets require apheresis, washing to remove antibody and irradiation to prevent graft versus host disease; they take time and are used if human platelet antigen matched platelets are unavailable. Corticosteroids have limited evidence in the neonate. (Source: British Society for Haematology Guideline on Neonatal Alloimmune Thrombocytopenia)
source_refs: British Society for Haematology Guideline on Neonatal Alloimmune Thrombocytopenia

options.text: Observe with serial platelet counts at 6 hourly intervals; transfuse only if platelets fall below 5 x10^9/L or bleeding worsens
options.rationale: Severe thrombocytopenia in a neonate with intracranial haemorrhage risk requires urgent transfusion regardless of clinical bleeding; the intracranial haemorrhage risk (10 to 20 percent, often in utero) mandates prompt correction. (Source: British Society for Haematology Guideline on Neonatal Alloimmune Thrombocytopenia)
source_refs: British Society for Haematology Guideline on Neonatal Alloimmune Thrombocytopenia

options.text: Transfuse pooled fresh frozen plasma 15 mL/kg intravenously over the next 30 minutes as the sole immediate intervention today
options.rationale: Fresh frozen plasma does not correct platelet count and is not appropriate treatment for immune thrombocytopenia. (Source: British Society for Haematology Guideline on Neonatal Alloimmune Thrombocytopenia)
source_refs: British Society for Haematology Guideline on Neonatal Alloimmune Thrombocytopenia

explanation.summary: Neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia presents with severe isolated thrombocytopenia in an otherwise well neonate of a mother with a normal platelet count, most commonly due to maternal antibody against foetal HPA-1a inherited from the father. Intracranial haemorrhage risk is 10 to 20 percent, often in utero, and can occur despite in utero intravenous immunoglobulin. Treatment of severe thrombocytopenia (<30 x10^9/L) is human platelet antigen matched (HPA-1a negative) platelet transfusion plus intravenous immunoglobulin 1 g/kg. Maternal washed and irradiated apheresis platelets are a backup. Antenatal management of subsequent pregnancies with weekly maternal intravenous immunoglobulin from 20 to 26 weeks is standard.
key_points: Neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia: severe isolated thrombocytopenia in a well neonate with a maternal normal platelet count.
Treatment: HPA-1a negative platelets plus intravenous immunoglobulin 1 g/kg.
Intracranial haemorrhage risk is 10 to 20 percent, often in utero, mandating urgent transfusion at platelets below 30 x10^9/L.
explanation.pearls: Severe neonatal thrombocytopenia (platelets 15) with a well mother and no maternal platelet drop is neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia: HPA-1a negative platelets plus intravenous immunoglobulin 1 g/kg immediately.

sources.label: British Society for Haematology Guideline on Neonatal Alloimmune Thrombocytopenia
International Collaboration on Fetal and Neonatal Alloimmune Thrombocytopenia recommendations

subtopic_detail: Severe combined immunodeficiency unmasked by live rotavirus vaccine complication after routine immunisation
stem:
You are the paediatric infectious diseases registrar reviewing a 5 month old boy admitted with 6 weeks of watery diarrhoea and failure to thrive following his routine 6 week and 4 month rotavirus vaccine (RotaTeq). He has severe faltering growth (weight fallen from 25th to below 3rd centile), oral candidiasis and a persistent low grade cough with hypoxia to 92 percent on room air. There is no family history of consanguinity. There is a maternal history of an infant sibling who died at 8 months of age of a respiratory infection; postmortem was inconclusive.

Investigations show lymphopenia (absolute lymphocyte count 0.6 x10^9/L). Chest computed tomography demonstrates diffuse ground glass with cystic changes suggestive of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia. Bronchoalveolar lavage shows Pneumocystis jirovecii and cytomegalovirus positive by polymerase chain reaction. Stool polymerase chain reaction shows vaccine strain rotavirus positive. His mother has not yet been offered chorionic villus sampling or newborn screening (SCID is not in state newborn screening panel).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148 /min, blood pressure 78/46 mmHg, respiratory rate 42 /min, SpO2 92% on room air, temperature 38.2 degC
data_table.Examination: Cachectic, small for age, oral thrush, mild hepatomegaly, subcostal recession, bilateral fine crackles
data_table.Investigations: Absolute lymphocyte count 0.6 x10^9/L, immunoglobulins IgG 1.2 g/L (3.0-9.0), IgA <0.05, IgM 0.2, T cell receptor excision circles absent, T cell subsets CD3 0.02 x10^9/L, CD19 0.15 x10^9/L, natural killer 0.05 x10^9/L, HIV negative

lead_in: Which single immediate management priority best addresses both his acute deterioration and definitive treatment planning?

options.text: Commence trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole treatment dose plus ganciclovir plus fluid resuscitation only; defer immunology referral to outpatient clinic
options.rationale: Treating opportunistic infections alone without immediate immunology and transplant referral misses the diagnosis window; severe combined immunodeficiency mortality without haematopoietic stem cell transplant is 100 percent by 2 years. (Source: European Society for Immunodeficiencies SCID Guideline)
source_refs: European Society for Immunodeficiencies SCID Guideline

options.text: Discharge on home oxygen with a plan for oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis and monthly monitoring at general practice
options.rationale: Home discharge is unsafe with severe combined immunodeficiency and active Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia and cytomegalovirus and vaccine strain rotavirus enteritis; specialist inpatient management with isolation is essential. (Source: European Society for Immunodeficiencies SCID Guideline)
source_refs: European Society for Immunodeficiencies SCID Guideline

options.text: Protective isolation, all cellular blood products irradiated cytomegalovirus negative, urgent immunology and transplant referral for donor search
options.rationale: Severe combined immunodeficiency confirmed by absent T cell receptor excision circles and profoundly low CD3, CD19 and natural killer cells requires immediate protective isolation, use of irradiated cytomegalovirus negative cellular blood products (to prevent transfusion associated graft versus host disease), Pneumocystis jirovecii prophylaxis, intravenous immunoglobulin replacement, avoidance of all live vaccines and urgent haematopoietic stem cell transplant workup because untreated mortality is close to 100 percent by 2 years. (Source: European Society for Immunodeficiencies SCID Guideline)
source_refs: European Society for Immunodeficiencies SCID Guideline

options.text: Continue routine immunisation schedule with the 6 month rotavirus dose plus a live measles-mumps-rubella catch up immunisation at 12 months
options.rationale: Live vaccines are contraindicated in severe combined immunodeficiency; live rotavirus, bacillus Calmette-Guerin, oral polio, varicella and measles-mumps-rubella vaccines can cause disseminated vaccine strain disease. (Source: European Society for Immunodeficiencies SCID Guideline)
source_refs: European Society for Immunodeficiencies SCID Guideline

options.text: Trial oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg/day for 4 weeks for presumed post infectious eosinophilic enteropathy pending further immunology testing
options.rationale: Corticosteroids in undiagnosed severe combined immunodeficiency will worsen opportunistic infections; the priority is diagnosis and transplant referral. (Source: European Society for Immunodeficiencies SCID Guideline)
source_refs: European Society for Immunodeficiencies SCID Guideline

explanation.summary: Severe combined immunodeficiency is a paediatric emergency with mortality close to 100 percent by age 2 without haematopoietic stem cell transplant. Live vaccines including rotavirus, bacillus Calmette-Guerin, oral polio, varicella and measles-mumps-rubella can cause disseminated vaccine strain disease and must be avoided. Diagnosis is confirmed by absent T cell receptor excision circles and profoundly low CD3 (and often CD19 and natural killer) counts. Management is immediate protective isolation, Pneumocystis jirovecii prophylaxis, intravenous immunoglobulin replacement, treatment of opportunistic infections, irradiated cytomegalovirus negative cellular blood products, and urgent haematopoietic stem cell transplant. Family counselling is essential for future pregnancies; T cell receptor excision circle newborn screening is now standard in several AU jurisdictions.
key_points: Severe combined immunodeficiency requires urgent haematopoietic stem cell transplant; untreated mortality is close to 100 percent by 2 years.
All cellular blood products must be irradiated and cytomegalovirus negative.
All live vaccines (rotavirus, bacillus Calmette-Guerin, oral polio, varicella, measles-mumps-rubella) are contraindicated.
explanation.pearls: Severe combined immunodeficiency (absent T cell receptor excision circles, CD3 <0.05, and vaccine strain rotavirus enteritis): protective isolation, irradiated cytomegalovirus negative blood products, Pneumocystis prophylaxis and urgent haematopoietic stem cell transplant workup.

sources.label: European Society for Immunodeficiencies SCID Guideline
Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Primary Immunodeficiency Guideline

subtopic_detail: Elective delivery timing and mode in asymptomatic placenta praevia at term
stem:
You are the obstetrics registrar reviewing a 34 year old woman gravida 3 para 2 at 34 weeks gestation with a persistent complete anterior placenta praevia confirmed on transvaginal ultrasound at 32 weeks. She has had no vaginal bleeding. She has two previous uncomplicated vaginal births at term. She has no other medical history. She has been counselled about risk of antepartum haemorrhage. She has been asked to avoid intercourse and heavy lifting.

She attends the antenatal high risk clinic today asking about delivery timing and mode. Magnetic resonance imaging showed no features of morbidly adherent placenta. Her booking blood group is O positive with negative antibody screen. Her partner is A positive. She has iron and folate supplementation. Her haemoglobin is 118 g/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84 /min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Examination: Uterus soft, fundus at 34 weeks, symphysis fundal height 33 cm, foetal heart 148 /min regular, no vaginal blood on outer clothing at review
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound complete anterior placenta praevia, cervix 3.4 cm closed, foetal biometry on 50th centile, umbilical artery Doppler normal, magnetic resonance imaging no features of morbidly adherent placenta

lead_in: What is the most appropriate delivery plan?

options.text: Elective caesarean at 36+0 weeks with a cell salvage strategy in place, plus antenatal betamethasone before caesarean
options.rationale: 36+0 is earlier than the RANZCOG recommended timing for asymptomatic placenta praevia and requires antenatal steroids because of prematurity risk; timing without prior bleeding is 36+0 to 37+6 in some guidance but Australian practice defaults to 37+0 to 37+6 for asymptomatic praevia. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta Guideline

options.text: Elective caesarean at 37+0 to 37+6 weeks; no antenatal betamethasone required unless earlier delivery becomes necessary before 37 weeks
options.rationale: Asymptomatic placenta praevia is delivered by elective caesarean at 37+0 to 37+6 weeks in AU per RANZCOG. Antenatal betamethasone is not routinely given if delivery is planned at 37 weeks or later. If earlier delivery becomes necessary (bleeding, preterm labour) before 34+6 weeks, a betamethasone course is given. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta Guideline

options.text: Elective caesarean at 39+0 weeks with a plan for expectant induction of labour if she goes into labour before then
options.rationale: 39+0 is too late for placenta praevia because of the accumulating risk of unplanned antepartum haemorrhage requiring emergency caesarean; 37 to 37+6 is standard. Induction is contraindicated in complete praevia. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta Guideline

options.text: Trial of vaginal delivery from 39+0 weeks because she has two previous uncomplicated vaginal births at term without complication
options.rationale: Vaginal delivery is contraindicated in complete placenta praevia regardless of parity; caesarean is mandated. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta Guideline

options.text: Elective caesarean at 34+0 weeks with a plan for antenatal betamethasone plus magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection given prematurity
options.rationale: 34+0 is inappropriately early without a clinical trigger and exposes the neonate to prematurity morbidity; timing is 37 to 37+6 unless bleeding or other complication mandates earlier delivery. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta Guideline

explanation.summary: Asymptomatic placenta praevia at term is delivered by elective caesarean at 37+0 to 37+6 weeks in AU per RANZCOG, balancing the maternal risk of antepartum haemorrhage against neonatal prematurity morbidity. Symptomatic praevia (bleeding) or high risk features (previous bleed, low anterior placenta with previous caesarean) may prompt delivery from 34 to 36+6 weeks, in which case antenatal betamethasone is given. Cell salvage, cross matched blood, senior obstetric and anaesthetic involvement and a written surgical plan are standard for high risk cases. Vaginal delivery is contraindicated in complete praevia regardless of parity. Magnetic resonance imaging is used to assess for accreta if the placenta is anterior and overlies a previous scar.
key_points: Elective caesarean at 37+0 to 37+6 weeks in asymptomatic praevia.
Antenatal betamethasone if delivery is expected before 34+6 weeks.
Vaginal delivery is contraindicated in complete placenta praevia regardless of parity.
explanation.pearls: Asymptomatic complete placenta praevia at term: elective caesarean at 37+0 to 37+6 weeks; antenatal betamethasone reserved for expected delivery before 34+6 weeks.

sources.label: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta Guideline
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists Optimal Timing of Elective Birth statement

subtopic_detail: Atypical endometrial hyperplasia management in a postmenopausal woman keen to avoid surgery
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 62 year old woman with 6 months of postmenopausal bleeding. She has a body mass index of 34 kg/m^2 and is on metformin for type 2 diabetes. She has no personal history of breast cancer. She has no personal or family history of endometrial or ovarian cancer. She has never used hormone replacement therapy or tamoxifen. She is not a smoker. She has hypertension on ramipril. She has completed her family. She is asking about non surgical options.

Transvaginal ultrasound showed an endometrial thickness of 14 mm. Hysteroscopy with directed biopsy has returned reporting atypical endometrial hyperplasia (endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia); there is no invasive component identified on biopsy. Magnetic resonance imaging shows a normal appearing myometrium and no adnexal pathology. She is otherwise well.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82 /min, blood pressure 138/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 34 kg/m^2, abdomen soft, no palpable adnexal mass, cervix nulliparous appearing, no palpable inguinal lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound endometrial thickness 14 mm, hysteroscopy directed biopsy atypical hyperplasia (endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia), magnetic resonance imaging normal myometrium and adnexa, haemoglobin A1c 6.8 percent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line management?

options.text: Oral medroxyprogesterone acetate 20 mg daily for 6 months with hysteroscopy monitoring at 3 monthly intervals only
options.rationale: Oral medroxyprogesterone acetate is less effective than levonorgestrel intrauterine device for endometrial hyperplasia and does not avoid the need for hysterectomy in postmenopausal atypical hyperplasia. (Source: RANZCOG College Statement on Endometrial Hyperplasia)
source_refs: RANZCOG College Statement on Endometrial Hyperplasia

options.text: Levonorgestrel 52 mg intrauterine device with 3 month hysteroscopy monitoring and continued therapy for 12 months minimum
options.rationale: Conservative management with levonorgestrel intrauterine device is reserved for premenopausal women wishing to preserve fertility or those unfit for surgery; in a postmenopausal woman who has completed her family, hysterectomy is first line. (Source: RANZCOG College Statement on Endometrial Hyperplasia)
source_refs: RANZCOG College Statement on Endometrial Hyperplasia

options.text: Total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy is the definitive first line management for postmenopausal atypical endometrial hyperplasia
options.rationale: Atypical endometrial hyperplasia (endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia) carries a 25 to 40 percent coexisting invasive endometrial cancer rate at hysterectomy specimen and a high progression risk to invasive cancer. In a postmenopausal woman who has completed her family, total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy is the definitive first line treatment. Conservative levonorgestrel intrauterine device therapy is reserved for premenopausal women wishing to preserve fertility or those unfit for surgery. (Source: RANZCOG College Statement on Endometrial Hyperplasia)
source_refs: RANZCOG College Statement on Endometrial Hyperplasia

options.text: Reassure and offer 6 monthly transvaginal ultrasound with an endometrial thickness cut off of 5 mm as her indication to repeat biopsy
options.rationale: Surveillance without treatment is inappropriate for atypical hyperplasia in a postmenopausal woman; hysterectomy is definitive and is first line. (Source: RANZCOG College Statement on Endometrial Hyperplasia)
source_refs: RANZCOG College Statement on Endometrial Hyperplasia

options.text: Endometrial ablation with second generation device balloon therapy in day surgery under general anaesthetic as definitive management
options.rationale: Endometrial ablation is not appropriate for treatment of atypical hyperplasia because it obscures future endometrial assessment and does not address coexisting invasive disease risk. (Source: RANZCOG College Statement on Endometrial Hyperplasia)
source_refs: RANZCOG College Statement on Endometrial Hyperplasia

explanation.summary: Atypical endometrial hyperplasia (endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia) carries a 25 to 40 percent risk of coexisting invasive endometrial cancer at hysterectomy and a high progression risk to invasive cancer. Total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy is the definitive first line treatment in postmenopausal women or women who have completed their family. Sentinel lymph node biopsy is considered at hysterectomy at some AU centres. Conservative levonorgestrel 52 mg intrauterine device management with 3 monthly hysteroscopy monitoring is reserved for premenopausal women who want to preserve fertility or women unfit for surgery. Non atypical hyperplasia is managed with progestogen and endometrial surveillance; regression is expected in more than 80 percent within 12 months.
key_points: Atypical hyperplasia: 25 to 40 percent coexisting endometrial cancer at hysterectomy specimen.
Postmenopausal atypical hyperplasia: total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy is first line.
Levonorgestrel intrauterine device conservative therapy reserved for premenopausal fertility preservation or unfit for surgery.
explanation.pearls: Postmenopausal atypical endometrial hyperplasia (endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia): total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy is definitive first line; the 25 to 40 percent coexisting endometrial cancer risk mandates surgery.

sources.label: RANZCOG College Statement on Endometrial Hyperplasia
European Society for Medical Oncology Endometrial Cancer Clinical Practice Guideline
